organism: Hepatitis B virus (HBV), a small double-stranded DNA virus in the family Hepadnaviridae. Infection is tracked through several serologic markers (HBsAg, anti-HBs, IgM/IgG anti-HBc, HBeAg/anti-HBe) rather than a single test. HBV is classified by both serologic subtype and genotype (A through J), which vary geographically and are associated with different transmission patterns and risk of long-term complications like cirrhosis and liver cancer. The virus remains infectious for at least 7 days on environmental surfaces, even without visible blood.
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is typically 60-90 days. Symptoms are more common in adults than in infants or young children, who are usually asymptomatic; about half of acutely infected adults are asymptomatic too. A nonspecific 3-10 day prodrome (fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine) precedes a 1-3 week icteric phase (jaundice, pale stools, hepatic tenderness), followed by weeks to months of convalescence. The central clinical fact about hepatitis B is the divide between acute and chronic outcomes: most adults who are infected clear the virus and recover completely, but as many as 90% of infants infected at birth or in infancy become chronically infected, versus 30%-50% of children infected between ages 1-5 and only about 5% of adults. Chronic infection is usually asymptomatic but is responsible for the large majority of HBV-related death and disability (cirrhosis, liver failure, liver cancer) - about 25% of people chronically infected as children, and 15% of those infected as adults, die prematurely from it. Fulminant hepatitis occurs in 1%-2% of acute adult infections.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the primary reservoir; some non-human primates in Africa and Southeast Asia are also infected. Transmission is via parenteral or mucosal exposure to HBsAg-positive body fluids - blood and serous fluids carry the highest concentration, with lower titers in saliva, tears, urine, semen, and breast milk. In the US, the most important routes are injection drug use, perinatal transmission, and sexual contact; fecal-oral transmission does not occur. There is no seasonal pattern. A person with acute or chronic infection is considered infectious any time HBsAg is detectable in blood.
secularTrendsSummary: Reported acute HBV incidence fell about 90% from 9.6 per 100,000 in 1982 (when vaccination recommendations began) to 1.0 per 100,000 in 2018, though under-ascertainment means the true 2018 case count was estimated at roughly 21,600 rather than the 3,322 reported. Incidence is now lowest in people 19 and younger (reflecting routine infant vaccination) and highest in adults 40-49; a 2009-2013 spike in Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia was tied to rising injection drug use. An estimated 850,000 to 2.2 million people in the US live with chronic HBV infection, the majority having immigrated from higher-endemicity countries. Globally, an estimated 257 million people are living with HBV infection, concentrated in parts of Asia, Africa, the Pacific Islands, the Middle East, and the Amazon Basin, where most infections are acquired at or shortly after birth.
vaccineDescription: The first recombinant HepB vaccine (Recombivax HB) was licensed in 1986, replacing an earlier plasma-derived vaccine; Engerix-B followed in 1989, and Heplisav-B, using a novel synthetic adjuvant, in 2017 for adults 18+. Recombinant vaccines cannot cause HBV infection since no infectious viral material is produced. HepB is also included in combination products: DTaP-HepB-IPV (Pediarix, children 6 weeks-6 years), DTaP-IPV-Hib-HepB (Vaxelis), and HepA-HepB (Twinrix, adults 18+). All are given intramuscularly, contain yeast protein and (except Heplisav-B) aluminum adjuvant, and some presentations contain latex.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Every medically stable infant weighing at least 2,000 g should receive the HepB birth dose within 24 hours of birth (using single-antigen vaccine only), followed by a routine 0, 1-2, 6-18 month schedule; the exact timing and whether HBIG is also needed depend heavily on maternal HBsAg status (see Perinatal Management). Unvaccinated children/adolescents through 18 get a 3-dose series at 0, 1, 6 months, with an alternative 2-dose Recombivax-HB-only option for ages 11-15 (0 and 4-6 months, completed before the 16th birthday). Adults use either a 2-dose Heplisav-B series (0, 1 month) or a 3-dose Engerix-B/Recombivax HB series (0, 1, 6 months); Twinrix follows its own 3-dose (0, 1, 6 months) or accelerated (0, 7, 21-30 days plus a 12-month booster) schedule. Minimum interval between doses 1 and 2 is 4 weeks; dose 3 must follow dose 2 by at least 8 weeks AND dose 1 by at least 16 weeks.
vaccineEfficacySummary: More than 90% of infants, children, adolescents, and adults under 40 develop a protective antibody response after a complete series, though immunogenicity declines with age (only about 75% by 60). Heplisav-B produces 90%-100% response after its 2-dose series. The birth dose plus HBIG is 85%-95% effective at preventing chronic infection in infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers; vaccine alone (without HBIG) is 70%-95% effective. Dialysis patients and other immunocompromised adults typically need larger or more numerous doses to seroconvert. Antibody levels decline over time, but immune memory persists for more than 30 years and protects against clinically significant infection even after measurable antibody has waned - so booster doses are not recommended for people with normal immune status.
contraindicationsSummary: A severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication, as is a documented history of hypersensitivity to yeast (a causal link between HepB vaccine and anaphylaxis in yeast-sensitive people was established in 2011; estimated incidence is 1.1 anaphylaxis cases per million doses). Moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution. Pregnancy is explicitly NOT a contraindication - available vaccines contain noninfectious HBsAg and pose no known infection risk to the fetus - though Heplisav-B specifically is not recommended in pregnancy for lack of safety data. Combination vaccines carry the contraindications of their individual components.
vaccineSafetySummary: Adverse events are mostly mild local or systemic reactions: pain (3%-29%), erythema (3%), swelling (3%), fever (1%-6%), and headache (3%). Rare reports of Guillain-Barre syndrome, chronic fatigue syndrome, various neurologic disorders, rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes, and other autoimmune disease have not been shown to have a causal link to the vaccine; scientific panel reviews have specifically found no causal association with multiple sclerosis. Rechallenge reports suggest the vaccine might very rarely trigger alopecia, though a population-based study found no statistically significant association.
vaccineStorageSummary: HepB vaccines must be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F). See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Hepatitis B is nationally notifiable in the US. Diagnosis depends on serologic testing rather than clinical presentation, since HBV infection can't be distinguished from other hepatitis on symptoms alone - which specific markers are present (HBsAg, anti-HBs, IgM/IgG anti-HBc, HBeAg) indicate whether infection is acute, chronic, resolved, or vaccine-induced. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for case-definition and investigation guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Perinatal Management
supplementalTopics.summary: Every infant born to an HBsAg-positive mother should receive both the HepB birth dose and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, in separate limbs; infants of mothers with unknown HBsAg status should get the birth dose within 12 hours and have the mother's status determined ASAP, with HBIG added within 7 days if she turns out positive. Pregnant women found HBsAg-positive should also be tested for HBV DNA; if levels exceed 200,000 IU/mL, antiviral therapy (tenofovir preferred) starting in the third trimester is recommended to further reduce transmission risk. For infants weighing under 2,000 g, the birth dose doesn't count toward the series because of reduced immunogenicity at that weight - they need 3 additional doses (4 total) starting at 1 month of chronologic age regardless of birth weight or gestational age by then. Infants born to HBsAg-positive or unknown-status mothers should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs at age 9-12 months, 1-2 months after finishing the series, to confirm protection.

supplementalTopics.title: Serologic Testing of Vaccine Recipients
supplementalTopics.summary: Prevaccination testing (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc) isn't required but can avoid unnecessarily vaccinating already-immune people in high-prevalence populations - it's specifically recommended for household/sexual/needle-sharing contacts of HBsAg-positive people, HIV-positive people, people with unexplained elevated liver enzymes, hemodialysis patients, MSM, and current or past injection drug users. It is NOT recommended before routine vaccination of infants, children, or adolescents. Postvaccination testing is not routine either, but is recommended when management depends on knowing immune status: infants of HBsAg-positive or unknown-status mothers, health care and public safety workers, hemodialysis patients, HIV-infected and other immunocompromised people, and sex partners of HBsAg-positive people. A result of anti-HBs 10 mIU/mL or higher, checked 1-2 months after the final dose, counts as immune.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccine Non-Response
supplementalTopics.summary: Older age (40+), male sex, obesity, diabetes, smoking, and chronic illness are all independently associated with failing to respond to the vaccine. Anyone who doesn't respond to the first series should complete a full second series (0, 1, 6 months) and be retested 1-2 months after finishing it. Fewer than 5% of people fail to develop detectable antibody after 6 total appropriately-administered doses; persistent non-responders should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBc, since chronic HBV infection is one reason for persistent non-response, and true non-responders who are HBsAg-negative should be counseled on precautions and on needing HBIG if they're later exposed.

supplementalTopics.title: Postexposure Management (Occupational and Non-Occupational)
supplementalTopics.summary: After a health care worker's needlestick or mucosal exposure, management depends on both the source patient's HBsAg status and the worker's own vaccination/response history: a documented responder needs no action regardless of source status, while an unvaccinated or non-responding worker exposed to a positive or unknown-status source needs HBIG plus vaccination (or revaccination). For non-occupational exposure to an HBsAg-positive source, an unvaccinated person should get both HBIG and vaccine as soon as possible (ideally within 24 hours, and unlikely to be effective much beyond 7 days for percutaneous or 14 days for sexual exposure), while someone with a documented complete series but no postvaccination testing needs only a single booster dose.

supplementalTopics.title: Adults Recommended for Vaccination
supplementalTopics.summary: ACIP recommends HepB vaccination for essentially any unvaccinated adult who is at risk or simply requests protection, without requiring them to disclose a specific risk factor. Named risk groups include: people at risk through sexual exposure (multiple partners, STI evaluation/treatment, MSM, sex partners of HBsAg-positive people); household contacts of HBsAg-positive people; people at risk of blood/body-fluid exposure (current/past injection drug use, health care and public safety workers, residents/staff of developmental-disability facilities); people with end-stage renal disease; people with diabetes age 19-59 (60+ at clinician discretion); people with hepatitis C or chronic liver disease; international travelers to higher-endemicity regions; people with HIV; and incarcerated people. In settings where a high proportion of adult patients are at risk (STI/HIV clinics, substance-use treatment, correctional facilities), ACIP recommends vaccinating all unvaccinated adults rather than screening for individual risk factors.

keyPoints: Formerly called 'serum hepatitis'; the first recorded cases followed smallpox vaccination with human-lymph-contaminated material in 1883
The younger a person is at infection, the more likely it becomes chronic - up to 90% of infants infected at birth versus about 5% of adults
Chronic infection, usually asymptomatic, causes the large majority of HBV-related death and disability, not acute illness
The birth dose is central to US prevention strategy and its exact timing/HBIG pairing depends on maternal HBsAg status, infant birth weight, and gestational stability
Booster doses are not recommended for immunocompetent people even as antibody levels decline, since immune memory persists 30+ years
An estimated 850,000-2.2 million people in the US live with chronic HBV infection, mostly people who immigrated from higher-endemicity countries
Pregnancy is explicitly not a contraindication to vaccination
